contextual_paragraphs.html: Flow-Matching (FM)-based zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems exhibit high-quality speech synthesis and robust generalization capabilities. However, the speaker representation ability of such systems remains underexplored, primarily due to the lack of explicit speaker-specific supervision in the FM framework. To this end, we conduct an empirical analysis of speaker information distribution and reveal its non-uniform allocation across time steps and network layers, underscoring the need for adaptive speaker alignment. Accordingly, we propose Time-Layer Adaptive Speaker Alignment (TLA-SA), a loss that enhances speaker consistency by jointly leveraging temporal and hierarchical variations in speaker information. Experimental results show that TLA-SA significantly improves speaker similarity compared to baseline systems on both research- and industrial-scale datasets and generalizes effectively across diverse model architectures, including decoder-only language models (LM) and FM-based TTS systems free of LM.
Index Terms—  Text-to-speech, flow matching, time and layer adaptation, speaker alignment

Driven by the advances in large-scale datasets and model scaling, modern Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems have achieved remarkable zero-shot generation, enabling them to synthesize speech for unseen speakers without fine-tuning. These models excel at capturing speaker characteristics, such as timbre and prosody, thereby enhancing their utility in real-world scenarios.

Most state-of-the-art FM-based TTS models  [arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3, arxiv2025-zhousiyi-indextts2, arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts] are based on Flow-Matching (FM) due to its strong modeling power and generalization capability. The use of FM modules in mainstream TTS systems falls into two paradigms: (1) conditioned on upstream intermediate representations (e.g., LM-generated tokens) to learn token-to-spectrogram mappings; (2) conditioned only on text (with optional prompts) to directly generate spectrograms. In the first type, the FM module takes input from a speech-text LM, such as  [arxiv2024-duzhihao-cosyvoice, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3, arxiv2025-zhousiyi-indextts2, arxiv2025-zhangbowen-minimax] . The CosyVoice series  [arxiv2024-duzhihao-cosyvoice, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3] integrates a text-speech LM with an FM decoder, achieving high naturalness and quality with low inference latency. IndexTTS2  [ arxiv2025-zhousiyi-indextts2 ] enhances speech duration control and disentangles speaker identity from emotion, enabling precise control over duration, timbre, and affect. Minimax  [ arxiv2025-zhangbowen-minimax ] further introduces a learnable speaker encoder and an auxiliary FM module, yielding strong zero-shot generalization and generation quality. In the second type, the FM TTS model generates Mel spectrogram conditioned on text and speech  [icassp2024-yiweiguo-voiceflow, slt2024-eskimez-e2tts, acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts] without a LM. VoiceFlow  [ icassp2024-yiweiguo-voiceflow ] introduces a rectified FM algorithm that enhances generation efficiency. E2-TTS  [ slt2024-eskimez-e2tts ] enables end-to-end FM-based TTS by padding blank tokens during generation. F5-TTS  [ acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts ] improves E2-TTS by incorporating an additional text encoder and a tailored sampling strategy, achieving strong performance with high real-time efficiency.

Despite the success of FM-based frameworks, their training objective is limited: the standard loss implicitly models the high-dimensional speech distribution without explicitly enforcing perceptual attributes such as speaker identity. This often results in insufficient refinement of fine-grained features in zero-shot scenarios, e.g., speaker similarity. Auxiliary supervision is a promising direction to explicitly guide such attributes. Prior work  [iclr2025-yusihyun-repa, is2025-jeongsoo-f5tts_ctc_speaker_areg, arxiv2025-tri-taro] shows that external representation alignment applied to intermediate FM features can accelerate convergence and improve performance. In the context of TTS, previous work  [ is2025-jeongsoo-f5tts_ctc_speaker_areg ] aligns text and speech modalities to increase efficiency. However, two questions remain underexplored: (1) how speaker information distributes across denoising steps and hierarchical layers in FM-based TTS, and (2) how to best design and integrate speaker supervision to leverage this structure. We first analyze speaker information flow in FM-based models and find that it varies significantly across layers and timesteps, motivating adaptive alignment. We thus propose Time-Layer Adaptive Speaker Alignment (TLA-SA), which dynamically aligns latent FM representations with speaker embeddings from a pre-trained encoder, conditioned on both timestep and depth. Our contributions are threefold:

We propose the TLA-SA loss to enhance speaker consistency for zero-shot TTS. The proposed TLA-SA aligns intermediate representation of FM with a pre-trained encoder and integrates temporal and hierarchical information of FM, and thus provides a dynamic speaker supervision to TM-based TTS.

We present an analytical study revealing that speaker information in FM-based TTS is unevenly distributed across denoising steps and model layers, highlighting the necessity of time-layer adaptive alignment and providing insight for speaker modeling in FM-based TTS models.

Experimental results confirm that the proposed TLA-SA loss consistently improves speaker modeling across large-scale and small-scale dataset sizes and mainstream model architectures. To analyze the distribution of speaker information in the FM-based TTS model, we adopt the training-free Centered Kernel Nearest-Neighbor Alignment (CKNNA)  [ arxiv-huh-platonic ] criterion, which quantifies the similarity between two sets of embeddings. We first examine whether CKNNA faithfully reflects the speaker modeling quality of TTS models. For each baseline checkpoint at different training steps, we first assess speaker similarity using a pre-trained speaker encoder for B B synthesized utterances from one of our test sets. Simultaneously, we extract intermediate speaker representations from each layer of the checkpoint. Specifically, given the intermediate representation E i ∈ ℝ B × T × D E_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times D} from the i i -th layer of the FM model with N N layers, temporal mean pooling is applied to derive the speaker representation:

We extract speaker embeddings E SA ∈ ℝ B × D ′ E^{\text{SA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D^{\prime}} from corresponding B B prompt speech in a test set with 37 distinct speakers and 500 utterances with the same encoder. We utilize CKNNA score of E i Speaker E_{i}^{\text{Speaker}} and E SA E^{\text{SA}} to reflect the distribution of speaker information at i i -th layer. As shown in Figure  2 , CKNNA exhibits a strong correlation with speaker similarity performance, validating its efficacy for analyzing speaker information.

We analyze the distribution of speaker information in the baseline FM model using CKNNA and observe significant non-uniformity across denoising times and layers  Figure 3 . Along the temporal dimension, we observe that speaker information is predominantly encoded during the initial denoising steps (t→0), where noise levels are highest. This observation is consistent with the understanding that the early stages of the diffusion prioritizes establishing global characteristics like speaker identity. As for hierarchical dimension, outputs of layers differ in their capacity to represent speaker information, with the final layers being particularly weak. Results indicate that a fixed and uniform supervision strategy is suboptimal, as it fails to adapt to these dynamics. This motivates an adaptive supervision scheme that accounts for both timestep and layer when enhancing speaker modeling.

We introduce Time-Layer Adaptive Speaker Alignment (TLA-SA), which facilitates both temporal and hierarchical information to boost speaker modeling in FM-based TTS. The key idea is to align intermediate representations of the FM module with embeddings extracted from a pre-trained speaker encoder. The speaker alignment loss at layer i i , denoted by ℒ i SA \mathcal{L}^{\text{SA}}_{i} , minimizes the discrepancy between E i Speaker E^{\text{Speaker}}_{i} , as mentioned in  Equation 3 , and the speaker alignment embedding E SA ∈ ℝ B × D ′ E^{\text{SA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D^{\prime}} of a pre-trained speaker encoder:

where 𝒟 ​ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \mathcal{D}(\cdot,\cdot) is a distance function and MLP i Layer \text{MLP}^{\text{Layer}}_{i} is one of N N layer adapters that projects E i Speaker E^{\text{Speaker}}_{i} into a shared latent space with E SA E^{\text{SA}} . To integrate temporal information into the hierarchical speaker alignment process, we employ the denoising time-step to predict a list of weights 𝐰 ∈ ℝ B × N \mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N} , which combine layer-wise SA losses across n n blocks. At denoising time t t , an embedding layer Emb Time \text{Emb}^{\text{Time}} outputs the time embedding, followed by the time adapter MLP Time \text{MLP}^{\text{Time}} produces these weights, through a softmax over the layer dimension:

Training Paradigm. To evaluate the effectiveness and generalization of TLA-SA, we experiment with two FM-based TTS architectures. LM-based FM TTS. Following CosyVoice 2  [ arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2 ] , the model comprises a speech-text language model and a Transformer U-Net CFM decoder with 2 down-sampling layers, 12 middle layers, and 2 up-sampling layers. TLA-SA supervision is applied to the middle layers. LM-free FM TTS. We utilize an FM-based TTS model with a transformer-based text encoder and 9 MMDiT  [ icml2024-esser-mmdit ] decoder layers, which is similar to  [ acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts ] .

Training Configuration. All models are trained from scratch on utterances with 24kHz sampling rate. A cosine learning rate scheduler with a 0.25-epoch warm-up is used, and optimization is performed with AdamW  [ arxiv2017-loshchilov-adamw ] ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 ). For TLASA-100k, models are trained for 156k steps with batch size 16 and gradient accumulation of 4. The learning rate decays from 8e-4 to 1e-6. For LibriTTS, models are trained for 125k steps with batch size 16, no gradient accumulation, and a learning rate decaying from 2e-4 to 1e-4. Unless specified, we use a WavLM-based  [ taslp2022-chensanyuan-wavlm_sv ] model fine-tuned on speaker verification task for the TLA-SA loss.

WER/CER. We evaluate Word Error Rate (WER) for English test sets and Character Error Rate (CER) for Mandarin test sets, using the speech recognition models provided by Seed-TTS  [ arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts ] . Speaker Similarity (SS) . We measure the similarity between generated speech and the prompt speech using the cosine similarity of their embeddings. Two pre-trained models are used: a speaker-related fine-tuned WavLM  [ arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts ] ( Sim-WavLM ) and the ERes2Net  [ icassp2025-chenyafeng-3dspeaker ] model from CosyVoice 2  [ arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2 ] ( Sim-ERes2Net ).

As shown in  Figure 4 , TLA-SA improves speaker similarity by 2.2% on Sim-WavLM, enhancing speaker modeling in FM-based TTS. Furthermore, it accelerates convergence by 2.9 × 2.9\times on the large-scale TLASA-100k dataset, demon strating its efficacy in guiding speaker representation learning.

Table 1 shows that TLA-SA improves speaker similarity by 3.0% (WavLM) and 2.1% (ERes2Net) on average compared to our model without TLA-SA, with negligible impact on CER/WER. These results confirm that TLA-SA provides an effective yet simple approach to improving speaker modeling during pre-training, consistent with our findings in  Figure 3 that the model with TLA-SA shows stronger speaker modeling capability. Free of speaker SFT stage, our CosyVoice 2 significantly outperforms FireRedTTS, which not only incorporates 50% additional data but also a SFT stage, demonstrating that TLA-SA offers a simple yet effective method to improve speaker modeling ability. Moreover, the TLA-SA boosted model achieves comparable performance to the official CosyVoice 2 with 50.0%, with a gap of only 2.1% on average against the model trained with 2 × 2\times data and SFT.

We evaluate on the high-quality LibriTTS dataset, which consists of only 0.6% of TLASA-100k. As shown in Table  2 , applying TLA-SA consistently improves speaker similarity by 2.8% and 2.5% (0.538 vs. 0.510, 0.596 vs. 0.571) on WavLM and ERes2Net, using supervision from a single pre-trained speaker encoder. These results indicate that TLA-SA enhances general speaker modeling rather than overfitting to specific evaluation models. Moreover, gains from layer and time adaptation underscore the importance of jointly leveraging temporal and hierarchical information for effective speaker alignment in FM-based TTS models.

Furthermore, we visualize the adaptive weight w w across time steps and model layers. As shown in   Figure 5 , TLA-SA loss applies selective supervision strength along both time and layer axes, effectively incorporating temporal and hierarchical information, which is consistent with observations in  Figure 3 . Specifically, higher weights are assigned to shallow layers and later time steps, suggesting their greater importance in speaker modeling and the need for stronger speaker-specific supervision.

To assess the generalization capability of our approach across FM-based TTS architectures, we evaluate it on models employing a decoder-only LM (e.g., CosyVoice series  [arxiv2024-duzhihao-cosyvoice, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3] ) and those without a LM (e.g., E2-TTS  [ slt2024-eskimez-e2tts ] and F5-TTS  [ acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts ] ). As presented in Table  3 , the proposed TLA-SA consistently enhances speaker modeling performance in both settings, indicating a strong cross-architecture generalization. Furthermore, the proposed TLA-SA gains an absolute improvement on the LM-free architecture (6% vs. 2.8% on WavLM and 7.1% vs. 2.5% on ERes2Net), demonstrating that TLA-SA effectively assists the speaker modeling.

In this section, we search for the optimal speaker encoder of TLA-SA using LibriTTS. As shown in Table  4 , CAM++ and ERes2Net outperform the WavLM-based model while using 42.5 × 42.5\times and 46.4 × 46.4\times fewer parameters, indicating that the WavLM-based model contains less speaker information even with fine-tuning on speaker verification. Moreover, TLA-SA with CAM++ achieves comparable or superior performance to WavLM and ERes2Net (0.544 vs. 0.538, 0.609 vs. 0.606), highlighting that TLA-SA enhances general speaker modeling in FM-based TTS rather than merely transferring information from a specific speaker encoder.

In this work, we propose TLA-SA, a loss that leverages temporal and hierarchical speaker alignment to enhance speaker consistency in zero-shot FM-based TTS systems. By introducing joint alignment across time steps and model layers, TLA-SA effectively strengthens speaker modeling. TLA-SA improves speaker similarity on large- and small-scale datasets, enabling models to achieve comparable or superior performance without speaker-specific fine-tuning, regardless of the training data size. Furthermore, TLA-SA yields consistent improvement on both FM TTS models with and without a cascaded LM respectively, demonstrating strong generalization across architectures. Future work will extend TLA-SA to broader FM variants and explore additional alignment signals to further enhance TTS performance.

contextual_paragraphs.html: Flow-Matching (FM)-based zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems exhibit high-quality speech synthesis and robust generalization capabilities. However, the speaker representation ability of such systems remains underexplored, primarily due to the lack of explicit speaker-specific supervision in the FM framework. To this end, we conduct an empirical analysis of speaker information distribution and reveal its non-uniform allocation across time steps and network layers, underscoring the need for adaptive speaker alignment. Accordingly, we propose Time-Layer Adaptive Speaker Alignment (TLA-SA), a loss that enhances speaker consistency by jointly leveraging temporal and hierarchical variations in speaker information. Experimental results show that TLA-SA significantly improves speaker similarity compared to baseline systems on both research- and industrial-scale datasets and generalizes effectively across diverse model architectures, including decoder-only language models (LM) and FM-based TTS systems free of LM.

Driven by the advances in large-scale datasets and model scaling, modern Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems have achieved remarkable zero-shot generation, enabling them to synthesize speech for unseen speakers without fine-tuning. These models excel at capturing speaker characteristics, such as timbre and prosody, thereby enhancing their utility in real-world scenarios.

Most state-of-the-art FM-based TTS models  [arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3, arxiv2025-zhousiyi-indextts2, arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts] are based on Flow-Matching (FM) due to its strong modeling power and generalization capability. The use of FM modules in mainstream TTS systems falls into two paradigms: (1) conditioned on upstream intermediate representations (e.g., LM-generated tokens) to learn token-to-spectrogram mappings; (2) conditioned only on text (with optional prompts) to directly generate spectrograms. In the first type, the FM module takes input from a speech-text LM, such as  [arxiv2024-duzhihao-cosyvoice, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3, arxiv2025-zhousiyi-indextts2, arxiv2025-zhangbowen-minimax] . The CosyVoice series  [arxiv2024-duzhihao-cosyvoice, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3] integrates a text-speech LM with an FM decoder, achieving high naturalness and quality with low inference latency. IndexTTS2  [ arxiv2025-zhousiyi-indextts2 ] enhances speech duration control and disentangles speaker identity from emotion, enabling precise control over duration, timbre, and affect. Minimax  [ arxiv2025-zhangbowen-minimax ] further introduces a learnable speaker encoder and an auxiliary FM module, yielding strong zero-shot generalization and generation quality. In the second type, the FM TTS model generates Mel spectrogram conditioned on text and speech  [icassp2024-yiweiguo-voiceflow, slt2024-eskimez-e2tts, acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts] without a LM. VoiceFlow  [ icassp2024-yiweiguo-voiceflow ] introduces a rectified FM algorithm that enhances generation efficiency. E2-TTS  [ slt2024-eskimez-e2tts ] enables end-to-end FM-based TTS by padding blank tokens during generation. F5-TTS  [ acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts ] improves E2-TTS by incorporating an additional text encoder and a tailored sampling strategy, achieving strong performance with high real-time efficiency.

Despite the success of FM-based frameworks, their training objective is limited: the standard loss implicitly models the high-dimensional speech distribution without explicitly enforcing perceptual attributes such as speaker identity. This often results in insufficient refinement of fine-grained features in zero-shot scenarios, e.g., speaker similarity. Auxiliary supervision is a promising direction to explicitly guide such attributes. Prior work  [iclr2025-yusihyun-repa, is2025-jeongsoo-f5tts_ctc_speaker_areg, arxiv2025-tri-taro] shows that external representation alignment applied to intermediate FM features can accelerate convergence and improve performance. In the context of TTS, previous work  [ is2025-jeongsoo-f5tts_ctc_speaker_areg ] aligns text and speech modalities to increase efficiency. However, two questions remain underexplored: (1) how speaker information distributes across denoising steps and hierarchical layers in FM-based TTS, and (2) how to best design and integrate speaker supervision to leverage this structure. We first analyze speaker information flow in FM-based models and find that it varies significantly across layers and timesteps, motivating adaptive alignment. We thus propose Time-Layer Adaptive Speaker Alignment (TLA-SA), which dynamically aligns latent FM representations with speaker embeddings from a pre-trained encoder, conditioned on both timestep and depth. Our contributions are threefold:

We propose the TLA-SA loss to enhance speaker consistency for zero-shot TTS. The proposed TLA-SA aligns intermediate representation of FM with a pre-trained encoder and integrates temporal and hierarchical information of FM, and thus provides a dynamic speaker supervision to TM-based TTS.

We present an analytical study revealing that speaker information in FM-based TTS is unevenly distributed across denoising steps and model layers, highlighting the necessity of time-layer adaptive alignment and providing insight for speaker modeling in FM-based TTS models.

Experimental results confirm that the proposed TLA-SA loss consistently improves speaker modeling across large-scale and small-scale dataset sizes and mainstream model architectures. To analyze the distribution of speaker information in the FM-based TTS model, we adopt the training-free Centered Kernel Nearest-Neighbor Alignment (CKNNA)  [ arxiv-huh-platonic ] criterion, which quantifies the similarity between two sets of embeddings. We first examine whether CKNNA faithfully reflects the speaker modeling quality of TTS models. For each baseline checkpoint at different training steps, we first assess speaker similarity using a pre-trained speaker encoder for B B synthesized utterances from one of our test sets. Simultaneously, we extract intermediate speaker representations from each layer of the checkpoint. Specifically, given the intermediate representation E i ∈ ℝ B × T × D E_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times D} from the i i -th layer of the FM model with N N layers, temporal mean pooling is applied to derive the speaker representation:

We extract speaker embeddings E SA ∈ ℝ B × D ′ E^{\text{SA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D^{\prime}} from corresponding B B prompt speech in a test set with 37 distinct speakers and 500 utterances with the same encoder. We utilize CKNNA score of E i Speaker E_{i}^{\text{Speaker}} and E SA E^{\text{SA}} to reflect the distribution of speaker information at i i -th layer. As shown in Figure  2 , CKNNA exhibits a strong correlation with speaker similarity performance, validating its efficacy for analyzing speaker information.

We analyze the distribution of speaker information in the baseline FM model using CKNNA and observe significant non-uniformity across denoising times and layers  Figure 3 . Along the temporal dimension, we observe that speaker information is predominantly encoded during the initial denoising steps (t→0), where noise levels are highest. This observation is consistent with the understanding that the early stages of the diffusion prioritizes establishing global characteristics like speaker identity. As for hierarchical dimension, outputs of layers differ in their capacity to represent speaker information, with the final layers being particularly weak. Results indicate that a fixed and uniform supervision strategy is suboptimal, as it fails to adapt to these dynamics. This motivates an adaptive supervision scheme that accounts for both timestep and layer when enhancing speaker modeling.

We introduce Time-Layer Adaptive Speaker Alignment (TLA-SA), which facilitates both temporal and hierarchical information to boost speaker modeling in FM-based TTS. The key idea is to align intermediate representations of the FM module with embeddings extracted from a pre-trained speaker encoder. The speaker alignment loss at layer i i , denoted by ℒ i SA \mathcal{L}^{\text{SA}}_{i} , minimizes the discrepancy between E i Speaker E^{\text{Speaker}}_{i} , as mentioned in  Equation 3 , and the speaker alignment embedding E SA ∈ ℝ B × D ′ E^{\text{SA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D^{\prime}} of a pre-trained speaker encoder:

Seed-TTS   [ arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts ] : A widely used zero-shot TTS evaluation set in Mandarin and English. For models trained on large-scale data, we evaluate on the test-zh and test-en subsets, containing 2,020 and 1,088 prompt-text pairs, respectively.

Training Configuration. All models are trained from scratch on utterances with 24kHz sampling rate. A cosine learning rate scheduler with a 0.25-epoch warm-up is used, and optimization is performed with AdamW  [ arxiv2017-loshchilov-adamw ] ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 ). For TLASA-100k, models are trained for 156k steps with batch size 16 and gradient accumulation of 4. The learning rate decays from 8e-4 to 1e-6. For LibriTTS, models are trained for 125k steps with batch size 16, no gradient accumulation, and a learning rate decaying from 2e-4 to 1e-4. Unless specified, we use a WavLM-based  [ taslp2022-chensanyuan-wavlm_sv ] model fine-tuned on speaker verification task for the TLA-SA loss.

WER/CER. We evaluate Word Error Rate (WER) for English test sets and Character Error Rate (CER) for Mandarin test sets, using the speech recognition models provided by Seed-TTS  [ arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts ] . Speaker Similarity (SS) . We measure the similarity between generated speech and the prompt speech using the cosine similarity of their embeddings. Two pre-trained models are used: a speaker-related fine-tuned WavLM  [ arxiv2024-anastassiou-seedtts ] ( Sim-WavLM ) and the ERes2Net  [ icassp2025-chenyafeng-3dspeaker ] model from CosyVoice 2  [ arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2 ] ( Sim-ERes2Net ).

Table 1 shows that TLA-SA improves speaker similarity by 3.0% (WavLM) and 2.1% (ERes2Net) on average compared to our model without TLA-SA, with negligible impact on CER/WER. These results confirm that TLA-SA provides an effective yet simple approach to improving speaker modeling during pre-training, consistent with our findings in  Figure 3 that the model with TLA-SA shows stronger speaker modeling capability. Free of speaker SFT stage, our CosyVoice 2 significantly outperforms FireRedTTS, which not only incorporates 50% additional data but also a SFT stage, demonstrating that TLA-SA offers a simple yet effective method to improve speaker modeling ability. Moreover, the TLA-SA boosted model achieves comparable performance to the official CosyVoice 2 with 50.0%, with a gap of only 2.1% on average against the model trained with 2 × 2\times data and SFT.

We evaluate on the high-quality LibriTTS dataset, which consists of only 0.6% of TLASA-100k. As shown in Table  2 , applying TLA-SA consistently improves speaker similarity by 2.8% and 2.5% (0.538 vs. 0.510, 0.596 vs. 0.571) on WavLM and ERes2Net, using supervision from a single pre-trained speaker encoder. These results indicate that TLA-SA enhances general speaker modeling rather than overfitting to specific evaluation models. Moreover, gains from layer and time adaptation underscore the importance of jointly leveraging temporal and hierarchical information for effective speaker alignment in FM-based TTS models.

Furthermore, we visualize the adaptive weight w w across time steps and model layers. As shown in   Figure 5 , TLA-SA loss applies selective supervision strength along both time and layer axes, effectively incorporating temporal and hierarchical information, which is consistent with observations in  Figure 3 . Specifically, higher weights are assigned to shallow layers and later time steps, suggesting their greater importance in speaker modeling and the need for stronger speaker-specific supervision.

To assess the generalization capability of our approach across FM-based TTS architectures, we evaluate it on models employing a decoder-only LM (e.g., CosyVoice series  [arxiv2024-duzhihao-cosyvoice, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice2, arxiv2025-duzhihao-cosyvoice3] ) and those without a LM (e.g., E2-TTS  [ slt2024-eskimez-e2tts ] and F5-TTS  [ acl2025-chenyushen-f5tts ] ). As presented in Table  3 , the proposed TLA-SA consistently enhances speaker modeling performance in both settings, indicating a strong cross-architecture generalization. Furthermore, the proposed TLA-SA gains an absolute improvement on the LM-free architecture (6% vs. 2.8% on WavLM and 7.1% vs. 2.5% on ERes2Net), demonstrating that TLA-SA effectively assists the speaker modeling.

In this section, we search for the optimal speaker encoder of TLA-SA using LibriTTS. As shown in Table  4 , CAM++ and ERes2Net outperform the WavLM-based model while using 42.5 × 42.5\times and 46.4 × 46.4\times fewer parameters, indicating that the WavLM-based model contains less speaker information even with fine-tuning on speaker verification. Moreover, TLA-SA with CAM++ achieves comparable or superior performance to WavLM and ERes2Net (0.544 vs. 0.538, 0.609 vs. 0.606), highlighting that TLA-SA enhances general speaker modeling in FM-based TTS rather than merely transferring information from a specific speaker encoder.

In this work, we propose TLA-SA, a loss that leverages temporal and hierarchical speaker alignment to enhance speaker consistency in zero-shot FM-based TTS systems. By introducing joint alignment across time steps and model layers, TLA-SA effectively strengthens speaker modeling. TLA-SA improves speaker similarity on large- and small-scale datasets, enabling models to achieve comparable or superior performance without speaker-specific fine-tuning, regardless of the training data size. Furthermore, TLA-SA yields consistent improvement on both FM TTS models with and without a cascaded LM respectively, demonstrating strong generalization across architectures. Future work will extend TLA-SA to broader FM variants and explore additional alignment signals to further enhance TTS performance.
